title: Watching a set being built
blurb: Each add() hashes the value to a slot, so the printed order is the slot order – not the insertion order – and it can reshuffle when the table grows.

notes.1: set() creates an empty set. Note: {} would have created an empty dict.
notes.2: 10 is hashed to a slot. With one element there is nothing to order yet.
notes.3: 20 lands in its own slot, found by hashing – no index was ever chosen by you.
notes.4: 30 is added. Python places it by hash, not at the 'end'.
notes.5: 40 is added. Compare the printed order with the insertion order 10, 20, 30, 40.
notes.6: 50 is added. The set now has 5 elements.
notes.7: 60 is added. The table is getting full; Python may grow it soon, which re-places every element.
notes.8: 70 is added. After a resize the iteration order can change completely.
notes.9: print shows the elements in slot order – this is the real iteration order, not insertion order.

title: Only hashable elements
blurb: A set can hold mixed immutable types, but a list (mutable, unhashable) is refused. (String positions can differ between runs because Python randomises string hashes.)

notes.2: A string is immutable and hashable, so it is accepted. Sets are heterogeneous.
notes.3: A tuple of immutables is hashable, so the whole tuple becomes ONE element.
notes.4: 20 is already present, so nothing changes – sets never keep duplicates, and no error is raised.
notes.5: A list is mutable and has no hash, so Python refuses it. Use a tuple instead: S.add((1, 2, 3)).

title: add, remove, discard, pop
blurb: remove() raises KeyError for a missing value, discard() stays silent, and pop() takes an arbitrary element. (String positions can differ between runs because Python randomises string hashes.)

notes.1: Notebook cell [20]: a set of five integers.
notes.2: add() inserts exactly one element. 'hi' is placed by hash, not at the end.
notes.4: 10 is not in the set. discard() ignores it silently.
notes.6: pop() takes no argument and removes an ARBITRARY element, returning it into x. Here it was the first element in slot order.
notes.7: 10 is not in the set. remove() raises KeyError, so wrap it in try/except or use discard().

title: Operations: new set vs update
blurb: union, intersection, difference and symmetric_difference return NEW sets. The _update variants change the set in place and return None.

notes.1: The first set from the lectures.
notes.2: The second set shares 5 and 7 with the first.
notes.3: union() builds a NEW set with every element once. s1 and s2 are untouched.
notes.4: intersection() keeps only the common elements 5 and 7, in a new set.
notes.5: difference() keeps elements of s1 that are not in s2.
notes.6: Difference is not commutative: s2 - s1 gives a different result.
notes.7: symmetric_difference() keeps elements that are in exactly one of the two sets.
notes.8: intersection_update() changes s1 IN PLACE: it now holds only 5 and 7. Nothing is returned.
notes.9: Rebind s1 to a fresh set so the next example starts clean.
notes.10: difference_update() modifies s1 in place and returns None – so r is None. Never write s1 = s1.difference_update(s2).

title: Alias vs copy() vs update()
blurb: alias = S1 is the SAME set with a second name; S1.copy() is an independent set. update() adds each item of an iterable.

notes.2: No copy: alias points to the very same set object.
notes.3: copy() creates a NEW, independent set with the same elements.
notes.4: add() changes the one set that S1 and alias both name. dup is unaffected.
notes.5: update() adds each item of the list separately: 60 and 70, not the list itself.
notes.6: alias shows every change made through S1.
notes.7: dup still has only the original three elements.
notes.8: clear() empties the shared set. S1 is still a set – it prints as set(), not {}.
notes.9: alias is empty too, because it is the same object.

title: Set comprehension, step by step
blurb: A set comprehension is a loop that adds each result to a set – duplicates collapse automatically. {x**2 for x in [...]} builds exactly this set in one line.

notes.2: The loop takes the next value from the list and stores it in x.
notes.3: x**2 is added. If the square is already in the set (4 and 1 appear twice), nothing changes – no error, no duplicate.
notes.4: S is {0, 1, 4}. The one-line form {x**2 for x in [-2, -1, 0, 1, 2]} gives the same set.
